note: The complete instruction set of obsign/replay/1. `number` is the row's ordinal in the canonical table (`OPS` in src/obsign_verify/replay.py) and is DOCUMENTATION ONLY: an instruction is encoded on the wire as a JSON array whose first element is the opcode NAME, a string, and whose remaining elements are JSON integers. The number never appears in a receipt. `kind` decides how the operands are validated and read, and is the same token the reference implementation uses so the two cannot drift.

operand_kinds.reg: a memory cell index; validated to 0 <= r < mem
operand_kinds.const: an index into `consts`; validated to 0 <= k < len(consts)
operand_kinds.target: an instruction index; validated to 0 <= t < len(code)
operand_kinds.frac: a fixed-point shift; validated to 0 <= f <= 63

validation_by_kind.loadc: operand 0 is a reg, operand 1 is a const
validation_by_kind.mulfx: operands 0..2 are regs, operand 3 is a frac
validation_by_kind.jump: the LAST operand is a target; every earlier operand is a reg
validation_by_kind.jcc: the LAST operand is a target; every earlier operand is a reg

opcodes.name: LOADC
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = consts[k]. The constant pool is validated as int64 at load time, so no wrap is needed here.

opcodes.name: MOV
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = mem[a].

opcodes.name: ADD
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = wrap(mem[a] + mem[b]). Wrapping int64: INT64_MAX + 1 is INT64_MIN.

opcodes.name: SUB
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = wrap(mem[a] - mem[b]).

opcodes.name: MUL
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = wrap(mem[a] * mem[b]). The product is formed EXACTLY (128 bits are enough for any int64 pair) and only then reduced modulo 2**64 into int64; a port that multiplies in native i64 and relies on hardware wrap lands on the same value, but one that multiplies in a double does not.

opcodes.name: DIV
opcodes.semantics: TRAP `division by zero` if mem[b] == 0. Otherwise mem[dst] = wrap(trunc(mem[a] / mem[b])), truncating TOWARD ZERO: -7 / 2 is -3, not -4. INT64_MIN / -1 leaves the range and WRAPS to INT64_MIN; it does not trap.

opcodes.name: MOD
opcodes.semantics: TRAP `modulo by zero` if mem[b] == 0. Otherwise mem[dst] = wrap(a - trunc(a / b) * b), so the remainder takes the sign of the DIVIDEND: -7 % 2 is -1.

opcodes.name: MIN
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = mem[a] if mem[a] < mem[b] else mem[b]. Signed comparison; no wrap is possible.

opcodes.name: MAX
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = mem[a] if mem[a] > mem[b] else mem[b].

opcodes.name: AND
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = wrap(mem[a] & mem[b]), bitwise on the two's-complement representation.

opcodes.name: OR
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = wrap(mem[a] | mem[b]).

opcodes.name: XOR
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = wrap(mem[a] ^ mem[b]).

opcodes.name: SHL
opcodes.semantics: TRAP `SHL shift amount B must be 0..63` unless 0 <= mem[b] <= 63. Otherwise mem[dst] = wrap(mem[a] << mem[b]): the shift is performed on the exact integer and the result reduced into int64, so bits shifted past bit 63 are discarded.

opcodes.name: SHR
opcodes.semantics: TRAP `SHR shift amount B must be 0..63` unless 0 <= mem[b] <= 63. Otherwise mem[dst] = wrap(mem[a] >> mem[b]), an ARITHMETIC right shift: the sign bit is propagated and the result FLOORS, so -3 >> 1 is -2. This is the one place the machine floors instead of truncating toward zero, and it is why DIV exists separately.

opcodes.name: EQ
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = 1 if mem[a] == mem[b] else 0.

opcodes.name: NE
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = 1 if mem[a] != mem[b] else 0.

opcodes.name: LT
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = 1 if mem[a] < mem[b] else 0. Signed.

opcodes.name: LE
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = 1 if mem[a] <= mem[b] else 0. Signed.

opcodes.name: GT
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = 1 if mem[a] > mem[b] else 0. Signed.

opcodes.name: GE
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = 1 if mem[a] >= mem[b] else 0. Signed.

opcodes.name: MULFX
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = wrap(trunc((mem[a] * mem[b]) / 2**frac)). THE ORDER IS THE SPECIFICATION: form the product EXACTLY at full width first, THEN truncate toward zero by 2**frac, THEN reduce into int64. Multiplying in int64 and shifting afterwards loses exactly the high bits the shift exists to discard -- the classic fixed-point porting bug -- and truncating with an arithmetic right shift floors instead, which differs for a negative product (-3 >> 1 is -2; truncation gives -1). `frac` is validated to 0..63, so the divisor is never zero and MULFX cannot trap.

opcodes.name: SEL
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = mem[a] if mem[cond] != 0 else mem[b]. Both arms are READ; this is a select, not a branch, and it costs one step either way.

opcodes.name: NEG
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = wrap(-mem[a]). NEG of INT64_MIN wraps back to INT64_MIN.

opcodes.name: ABS
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = wrap(abs(mem[a])). ABS of INT64_MIN is 2**63, which is outside int64 and wraps back to INT64_MIN. Stated because a port using a native abs on i64 may instead panic or invoke undefined behaviour there.

opcodes.name: NOT
opcodes.semantics: mem[dst] = wrap(~mem[a]), the bitwise complement: ~x == -x - 1.

opcodes.name: LOAD
opcodes.semantics: addr = mem[addr_reg]. TRAP `LOAD address ADDR out of bounds` unless 0 <= addr < mem. Otherwise mem[dst] = mem[addr]. The address is a RUNTIME value, so this is the one addressing mode the validator cannot bound statically.

opcodes.name: STORE
opcodes.semantics: addr = mem[addr_reg]. TRAP `STORE address ADDR out of bounds` unless 0 <= addr < mem. Otherwise mem[addr] = mem[src]. Note the operand ORDER: the address register comes first, the source second.

opcodes.name: JMP
opcodes.semantics: pc = target. The target is validated to be a real instruction index at load time, so a jump cannot leave the program.

opcodes.name: JMPZ
opcodes.semantics: if mem[cond] == 0 then pc = target; otherwise execution continues at the next instruction.

opcodes.name: JMPNZ
opcodes.semantics: if mem[cond] != 0 then pc = target; otherwise execution continues at the next instruction.

opcodes.name: HALT
opcodes.semantics: Stop. The output window is read from memory and returned. HALT COSTS ONE STEP: the budget is checked, the step counter is incremented and the pc is advanced before the opcode is dispatched, so a program of exactly one HALT retires 1 step and a program declaring `steps: 1` that is one HALT completes.
